contributions: On-policy self-distillation with no external supervision of any kind, using the model's own majority vote under a consistency threshold as the only signal.

The argument, supported by a controlled comparison at matched rollout budget, that a consensus answer should enter as privileged teacher context for token-level distillation rather than be reduced to a scalar reward -- with the reward-based label-free baselines gaining at most 1.5 percent where the context-based method gains 8.5 to 10.7.
Distillation restricted to the completions that disagree with the consensus, so the update targets exactly the cases where the model was confidently wrong.

A re-examination of objective choices under pseudo-labels rather than assuming they transfer, finding the preference for full-distribution divergence is stronger with noisy labels than with gold ones, and that top-100 truncation is free.

A characterised training collapse: reverse KL fails by progressive loss of termination rather than by incoherent reasoning, with generation length and answer-parsability curves reported through the failure.
A limitations section that quantifies its own regime dependence, names the accuracy of its pseudo-labels, and states which error bars are missing.
limitations: Stated fully and unusually well. Scope is one model family, two sizes, both modes, and one domain with automatically checkable answers -- and the voting mechanism requires an extractable canonicalisable answer, so extension to open-ended generation would need a softer consensus. The size of the advantage is explicitly called regime-dependent, with the authors instructing readers to treat consensus as a stronger replacement for gold solutions in the non-thinking regime and merely a match for them in the thinking regime rather than as a uniform improvement, and giving both sets of numbers to support that. Dependence on base competence is named as the structural bound: majority-vote supervision reproduces whichever answer the model already produces most often and is therefore capped by that answer's accuracy, with a probe measuring 13.3 percent wrong pseudo-labels in-domain and no experiment under deliberately corrupted votes. Variance is addressed by evaluating every checkpoint with twelve samples across five benchmarks, with the authors stating plainly that seed-replicated error bars for every training setup are pending and will be added in a revision. Not stated but worth noticing: the instruction-tuned comparison is favourable on average while the gold-supervised baseline leads on three of five benchmarks for one of the two models, which the authors report; and the self-consistency threshold that decides which prompts supply supervision is a hyperparameter whose sensitivity is not swept in the results reported here.
method: Several rollouts are sampled for a prompt and a pseudo-solution is constructed by majority vote subject to a self-consistency threshold, so a prompt with no clear consensus supplies no supervision. The pseudo-solution is then used as privileged context conditioning the teacher's distribution -- the same model, conditioned on the consensus answer -- and the student is distilled toward that conditioned distribution on the completions that disagreed with it, so the update lands precisely where the model was confidently wrong. The distinction the paper presses is that consensus enters as context for token-level distillation rather than as a reward signal, which is what separates it from the label-free reinforcement-learning baselines it compares against. Because the method changes the teacher's conditioning rather than the distillation objective, the paper revisits whether objective choices established under gold supervision still hold under pseudo-labels: full-vocabulary divergence against sampled-token distillation, top-k truncations of the vocabulary from 20 upward, and forward against reverse and symmetric divergences. Evaluation covers five competition-mathematics benchmarks on two model sizes in both a non-thinking and a thinking mode, plus two instruction-tuned models including a substantially larger mixture-of-experts one, against supervised fine-tuning, group-relative policy optimisation, supervised on-policy self-distillation, and three label-free reinforcement-learning methods under the same rollout budget.
one_liner: Removes external supervision from on-policy self-distillation by building a pseudo-solution from the model's own majority vote and using it as privileged teacher context rather than as a scalar reward, then distilling only on the completions that disagree with it.
problem: On-policy self-distillation is presented as self-supervised but is not: existing methods depend on ground-truth answers, environmental feedback, or a larger teacher model. The label-free reinforcement-learning alternatives that do without those signals reduce whatever consensus they extract to a scalar reward, which discards most of the information a consensus answer carries. The open question is whether a model's own generations contain enough structure to supervise it, and in what form that structure should be delivered.

relevance.reasoning-evaluation: The comparison at the centre of this paper is one the archive should record as a general point about signal design rather than as a result about distillation. Four methods extract the same thing -- a consensus answer over sampled rollouts -- and differ only in what they do with it. The three that compress it into a scalar reward gain at most 1.5 percent over base under the same rollout budget; the one that keeps it as conditioning context for a token-level objective gains 8.5 to 10.7. Whatever else is going on, that is a large penalty for reducing a structured signal to one number, and it sits alongside the archive's other evidence that outcome-only rewards collapse a trajectory into a bit. The paper is also a good model of not assuming a design choice transfers: because it changes the teacher's conditioning rather than the objective, it re-runs the objective comparisons under pseudo-labels and finds the preference for full-distribution divergence is roughly seven times stronger with noisy labels than with gold ones -- so a hyperparameter validated under clean supervision can be badly mis-set under noisy supervision, in the direction of underestimating how much it matters. Two things belong in the archive's evaluation practice. The reverse-KL collapse is a well-documented instance of a failure mode this archive keeps meeting: the model does not reason worse, it stops terminating, with generation length rising through 2.7k, 12k, 76k characters to the token ceiling while parsable-answer rate falls from 99 to 33 percent. Reporting the length and parsability curves through a failure is what distinguishes a diagnosis from a note that training diverged. And the limitations section is close to exemplary -- it quantifies its own regime dependence and tells the reader which conclusion to draw in each regime, states that its pseudo-labels are 13.3 percent wrong, names the experiment it did not run under corrupted votes, and says outright that seed-replicated error bars are pending. The structural bound it identifies is the one to carry: majority-vote supervision reproduces whichever answer the model already produces most often, so it is capped by that answer's accuracy and cannot teach anything the model does not already usually get right.

results: In non-thinking mode the method reaches averages of 49.49 and 54.31 at two scales, improving on the base models by 8.5 and 10.7 percent, taking the best result on four of five benchmarks at both sizes, and beating every supervised baseline including the gold-supervised version of itself by 3.2 and 2.3 percent -- while the three label-free reinforcement-learning baselines improve on base by at most 1.5 percent under the same rollout budget. That contrast is the paper's central claim, since all four methods extract the same consensus and differ in whether it becomes a token-level teacher context or a scalar reward. In thinking mode the same method gains only 2.2 and 1.9 percent and merely matches the gold-supervised version, which the authors attribute to the stronger base models leaving less headroom and to far longer rollouts meaning fewer completed votes per token of budget. The objective ablations are more informative than the headline. The full-vocabulary divergence beats sampled-token distillation by a wider margin under pseudo-labels than under gold supervision -- 17.8 and 7.2 percent on two benchmarks against 2.0 and 2.7 under gold -- so a preference established with real labels understates itself when the labels are noisy. Truncating the divergence to the teacher's top-100 entries matches or beats the full vocabulary on average, making it a free optimisation rather than a compromise. And the divergence-metric sweep produces a clean failure with a diagnosis: symmetric Jensen-Shannon divergence costs 13.8 percent and lands level with the untrained model, while reverse KL does not converge at all, collapsing gradually and one-directionally -- generations averaging 2.7 thousand characters at step 25, 12 thousand at 50, 76 thousand at 75 and hitting the token ceiling from step 125, with the fraction of rollouts producing a parsable answer falling from 99 to 33 percent. Inspection shows the failure is loss of termination rather than incoherent reasoning: a phrase, a bracket pair or a markup command repeated until the budget runs out.
